problems.title: finite squared-hinge penalties and exact feasibility
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 1-2, 6, Eqs. (8)-(9); its cited penalty-theory source arXiv:2410.03955v4, pp. 8-10, Assumptions 1-4 and Theorem 1.
claim: The discussion following Eq. (\(9\)) relates a finite squared-hinge KL penalty to the constrained KKT system, while the abstract/introduction describe trust-region enforcement.
analysis: At a feasible point, the gradient of \(\beta[D(\theta)-\delta]_+^2\) is zero. An active constrained optimum with a positive KKT multiplier can nevertheless have a nonzero objective gradient, so it need not be stationary for this finite penalty. For \(\pi_{\rm old}=(1/2,1/2)\), \(\pi_\theta=(\operatorname{sigmoid}\theta,1-\operatorname{sigmoid}\theta)\), \(J(\theta)=\theta\), and \(D(\theta)=\log\cosh(\theta/2)\), the constrained maximum is \(\theta_*=2\operatorname{arcosh}(e^\delta)\). At \(\delta=10^{-4}\) and \(\beta=1000\), \(\theta_*\simeq0.02828474\), whereas the penalized stationary maximum has \(\theta\simeq0.25371689\) and \(D\simeq0.00802504>\delta\). The bounded objective \(J(\theta)=2\tanh(\theta/2)\) similarly permits \(D\simeq0.00794101\).
result: Finite penalization alone does not imply exact hard feasibility. The cited penalty theorem concerns approximate KKT conditions with tolerance-dependent assumptions and schedules; that theorem is not refuted. Special instances can have exactly feasible penalized optima, so a literal existential claim that this can happen is also not refuted.
repair: State approximate stationarity/feasibility and the required assumptions. If exact feasibility is intended, provide an appropriate constrained-update argument. For the scalar example, \(\theta_*=2\operatorname{arcosh}(e^\delta)\) and \(\lambda_*=2/\tanh(\theta_*/2)\).
problems.impact_rationale: The finite penalty does not ensure hard feasibility, but the cited formal theorem already concerns approximate KKT conditions. This qualification does not refute that theorem or the empirical results.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: finite groups retain difficulty-dependent selection
problems.source_location: paper pages: 1 7 8 19; paper equations: 7 10; code: verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:289-314,377-400,470-503,571-602 verl/verl/trainer/config/ppo_trainer.yaml:159-166 scripts/train/run_disco_logL_1.5b_8k.sh
claim: The abstract and Table 1 describe complete removal of difficulty bias. The released loss excludes groups containing only one reward class and divides by the original question count.
analysis: Let a question have success probability \(p\), and let \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) be its number of correct responses. A mixed group is included with probability \(h_n(p)=1-p^n-(1-p)^n\). Since excluded groups contribute zero but the denominator remains the original question count, the expected finite-group contribution retains this difficulty-dependent factor. A question with one correct and one incorrect possible outcome already yields this construction for the full DRO objective. For \(n=8\), \(h_8(0.01)\simeq0.0772553\) and \(h_8(1/2)=0.9921875\); the relative inclusion weight is about \(0.0778636\). The cited configuration disables dynamic filtering, and the rejection-sampling flag defaults to false.
result: The finite fixed-group implementation does not completely remove difficulty-dependent question selection. The population decomposition correctly removes its explicit \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) factor, and the method can still provide useful practical reweighting.
repair: Restrict the claim to the population normalization and available mixed groups, or specify a justified question-level sampling/inclusion correction. Dividing by the number of valid groups alone does not equalize original-question inclusion.
problems.impact_rationale: Complete finite-group difficulty-bias removal is a central advertised property; the exact inclusion factor contradicts that universal property.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: a lower bound does not ensure monotonic improvement
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v5, Eqs.(7),(10), PDF pp.5,7, and paragraph following Eq.(10)
claim: The paragraph following Eq. (\(10\)) infers that increasing the lower bound \(J_2\le J_1\) automatically increases \(J_1\).
analysis: The witness has one question and three one-token outputs with rewards \(r(o_1)=1\), \(r(o_2)=r(o_3)=0\). Under the fixed old policy \((0.4,0.3,0.3)\), the conditional positive law is a point mass on \(o_1\), and the conditional negative law assigns \(1/2\) to each of \(o_2,o_3\). With the paper’s log-likelihood score \(s_\theta(o_i)=\log\pi_i\), Eqs.(7) and (10) reduce exactly to \[J_1(\pi)=\log\pi_1-\tfrac12(\log\pi_2+\log\pi_3),\] \[J_2(\pi)=\log\pi_1-\tau\log\{(\pi_2^{1/\tau}+\pi_3^{1/\tau})/2\}.\] The trust-region quantity is \(D_{\rm KL}(\pi_{\rm old}\|\pi)=\sum_i\pi_{{\rm old},i}\log(\pi_{{\rm old},i}/\pi_i)\).

Write \(J_1=J_2+G\), where \(G\ge0\). An increase in \(J_2\) can be outweighed by a decrease in \(G\). A policy-level example uses reference probabilities \((0.4,0.3,0.3)\), temperature \(\tau=10\), and candidate policies \(A=(0.4,0.305,0.295)\) and \[B=(0.4000318,0.2999841,0.2999841)\]. Substitution in the paper's objectives gives \(J_2(B)-J_2(A)\simeq7.481517\times10^{-6}>0\), but \(J_1(B)-J_1(A)\simeq-6.409938\times10^{-6}<0\). Their KL values are approximately \(8.334491\times10^{-5}\) and \(2.106713\times10^{-9}\), both below \(\delta=10^{-4}\).
result: The asserted monotonic implication is false even within the stated KL region. The lower bound and the entropic DRO variational identity can remain correct; practical superiority is a separate empirical question.
repair: Remove automatic monotonicity, or supply a touching-minorizer, gap-control or acceptance condition that actually controls \(J_1\).
problems.impact_rationale: A central theoretical explanation infers improvement of an objective from improvement of a non-touching lower bound. The policy-level counterexample directly reverses the claimed implication.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Relative objective/penalty signs in Algorithm 1
problems.source_location: paper pages: 19; algorithm lines: 9 10 11; code: verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py
claim: Algorithm 1 defines \(G_1\) as the objective gradient and \(G_2\) as the positive penalty gradient, then supplies \(G_1+G_2\) to the optimizer.
analysis: Descent on \(-J_2+P\) requires \(-G_1+G_2\); ascent requires \(G_1-G_2\). Adding both gradients gives the wrong relative sign under either convention. The author-released loss minimizes the negative objective plus the positive penalty, so its relative sign is correct.
result: Following pseudocode can give wrong direction; this does not establish wrong public loss or wrong reported training. Actual public objective/penalty relative sign is correct.
repair: For a descent optimizer, write \(-G_1+G_2\) and state the convention.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Printed and implemented penalty gradients differ by a factor of two
claim: Eq. (\(9\)) uses \(\beta[D-\delta]_+^2\), whose gradient is \(2\beta[D-\delta]_+\nabla D\).
analysis: In each cited implementation branch, the detached coefficient gives only \(\beta[D-\delta]_+\nabla D\). Detachment removes the coefficient derivative, making this the gradient of \((\beta/2)[D-\delta]_+^2\).
result: Numerical beta setting is not an exact Eq \(9\) reproduction; retuning can absorb factor, so less severe than sign error. Penalty direction is correct; beta is tunable.
repair: Use a consistent \(\beta/2\) convention or double the detached coefficient. Differentiating \(\beta\max(D-\delta,0)^2\) directly gives the printed gradient.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: MATH500 overlaps and duplicate training pairs
problems.source_location: paper pages: 7; data: deepscaler/deepscaler/data/train/deepscaler.json deepscaler/deepscaler/data/test/math.json datasets/deepscaler/data/train.parquet datasets/deepscaler/data/math.parquet
claim: Paper describes about \(40.3\) thousand unique pairs; delivered train/test files should identify benchmark separation.
analysis: The author-released MATH test indices \(80,285,412\) match training indices \(7202,7141,6976\) after Unicode NFKC normalization, whitespace normalization and case folding; the corresponding answers \(501,440,406\) agree. The first pair is also identical before normalization. JSON and Parquet problem orders agree. There are \(40\,315\) training rows but only \(39\,616\) raw unique problem-answer pairs, \(39\,387\) raw unique problems and \(39\,097\) normalized unique problems. The other five released test sets have no exact normalized match under this narrow comparison.
result: These are concrete overlaps in the delivered data, with no semantic/fuzzy matching claim. Even attributing all three MATH answers to overlap changes an individual six-set macro-score by at most \(0.1\) percentage point; this does not explain the full reported improvement.
repair: Correct counts; publish deduplicated/decontaminated manifests. Report sensitivity excluding \(3\) affected MATH questions; use clean future training release. Retraining is required to estimate causal effect of changing training data.
problems.impact_rationale: The overlaps are concrete, but their maximal contribution under the stated aggregate is small and cannot account for the main improvement.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Checkpoint selection and uncertainty: unresolved empirical scope
claim: Paper reports best performance and significant superiority without a complete selection manifest or uncertainty intervals.
analysis: The paper evaluates every \(200\) steps and reports best performance, without a fully specified independent checkpoint-selection rule. Its checklist openly reports no error bars. Averaging \(16\) correctness samples estimates pass@\(1\), rather than pass@\(16\), and does not measure training-seed variability. Dynamic sampling is disabled for all compared methods, which is disclosed. The fixed \(0.001\) KL ablation does not establish failure of every tuned regularizer.
result: Multiple models, six benchmarks and a second training dataset provide useful reported evidence. Checkpoint attribution and statistical robustness remain unresolved; no corrected effect size is supplied.
repair: Publish table/checkpoint/seed/config/dataset manifests and selection protocol. Compute paired question-level intervals from saved outputs; estimate training-seed uncertainty separately. Scope DAPO and stability comparisons to tested conditions.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Proposition 1's sign-dependent monotonicity
claim: Proposition 1 assumes f nondecreasing in x and remark says assumptions hold for GRPO.
analysis: For a negative reward \(y=-1\), the clipped branch is \(f(x,-1)=-\max(x,1-\varepsilon)\), which is nonincreasing. At \(\varepsilon=0.2\), \(f(1,-1)=-1\) and \(f(1.1,-1)=-1.1\), contradicting the claimed nondecreasing condition. The population decomposition itself does not require that extra condition.
result: Correct the sign-dependent assumption; the decomposition identity is not refuted.
repair: Remove extra monotonicity of f for all y; retain branchwise assumptions or state sign-dependent monotonicity.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.

problems.title: Dr. GRPO's relative question weighting
problems.source_location: paper pages: 4 5 20 21; paper figures: 1; paper equations: 19
claim: The text interprets \(p(1-p)\) as mitigating question imbalance relative to \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}\).
analysis: After normalizing both weights to one at \(p=1/2\), \(r_{\rm GRPO}(p)=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) and \(r_{\rm Dr}(p)=4p(1-p)=r_{\rm GRPO}(p)^2\). At \(p=0.01\), these are approximately \(0.1989975\) and \(0.0396\). Under the displayed relative-weight criterion, the latter attenuates extreme questions more strongly.
result: The interpretation of the relative weights is reversed. This does not determine empirical performance, and an overall gradient-scale change can be absorbed into the learning rate.
repair: Distinguish absolute scale from relative weighting and other definitions of bias; correct mitigation sentence under displayed criterion.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.
